case_name: Integrated Contractors Ltd. v. Leduc Development Ltd.
text:
IN
THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Integrated Contractors Ltd. v.
Leduc Development Ltd.,

2009 BCSC 965

Date: 20090622

Docket:
0729340

Registry: Prince George

Between:

Integrated Contractors Ltd.

Plaintiff

And

Leduc Development Ltd.

Defendant

And:

L
& M Engineering Limited

Defendant by Counterclaim

Before: The Honourable Madam Justice Griffin

Oral Ruling in Chambers

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

Karen L. Weslowski

Counsel for the Defendant:

Andrew J. Winstanley

Counsel for the Defendant by
Counterclaim:

Mitchell D. Houg

Place and Date of Hearing:

Vancouver, B.C.

May 27, June 22, 2009

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver, B.C.

June 22, 2009

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

This is an action arising out of a failed
residential development in Fort Nelson, BC.  There are three parties involved
in the litigation.  Two of them are defendants by counterclaim who have
parallel applications seeking an order that the defendant Leduc Development
Ltd. (“Leduc”) post security for costs in relation to its counterclaim.  One of
the applicants is also the plaintiff.

THE PARTIES AND NATURE OF THE CLAIMS AND
DEFENCES

[
2
]

The plaintiff, Integrated Contractors Ltd.
(“ICL”), is a contractor which performed work on a residential development
located in Fort Nelson, BC pursuant to a contract with the developer, the
defendant Leduc.

[
3
]

In its claim, ICL alleges that Leduc, as owner
of property in Fort Nelson, hired ICL as contractor to perform work on the
property.  ICL alleges it performed all of the work but it was not paid by
Leduc for this work.  Thus, in August 2006, ICL filed a claim of lien on the
property alleging that the sum of $275,544.19 was due and owing to it.  In its
claim, ICL relies on a written contract with Leduc dated October 4, 2005, as
well as an irrevocable direction to the Royal Bank of Canada from Leduc to pay
ICL, dated September 12, 2005.  ICL alleges that Leduc breached the terms of
the contract and additional work agreements, and breached the direction to
pay.  In the alternative, ICL alleges that Leduc misrepresented to ICL that it
would be paid in full accordance with the direction to pay.

[
4
]

In response, Leduc filed a statement of defence
and counterclaim.  In its statement of defence and counterclaim, Leduc alleges
that ICL had oral as well as written contracts with it, and that ICL repudiated
the contracts.  Leduc alleges this created a delay in the residential development
at a critical time and put economic duress on Leduc.  Leduc says this caused it
to enter into amendments to the contract with ICL, which are voidable.  Leduc
alleges that ICL has caused it to suffer damages as a result of its breaches of
contract.

[
5
]

Recently, in March 2009, Leduc amended its
statement of defence and counterclaim (the “amended counterclaim”) to add L
& M Engineering (“L & M”) as a defendant by counterclaim and to advance
additional allegations against ICL in the counterclaim.  L & M is an
engineering firm that was hired by Leduc to provide services with respect to
the development.

[
6
]

In essence, the nub of the expanded allegations
in the amendments is that by their wrongful acts, the defendants by
counterclaim, ICL and L & M, caused delay in the residential development
and an inability on the part of Leduc to close a transaction that would have
resulted in a sale of 23 of the 27 lots in phase one of the development.
According to the theory of the case advanced by Leduc, this created a domino
effect and has ultimately resulted in a foreclosure on the property that was
under development.

[
7
]

The expected length of trial is 20 days.  Both
ICL and L & M say that the allegations advanced by Leduc in the
counterclaim are complex and will require considerable time and effort to
defend.

PRIOR PAYMENT OF MONEY INTO COURT

[
8
]

Security for ICL’s lien claim, in the amount of
$275,544.19, has been posted in court.  In addition, Leduc has posted $30,000
as security for ICL’s costs.  This security was the result of certain steps
taken by ICL, which resulted in a garnishing order before judgment and then
negotiations with Leduc.  There is no prior judgment of this court dealing with
a contested application for security for costs in this proceeding.

APPLICABLE LEGAL PRINCIPLES

[
9
]

This application is governed by the provisions
of
s. 236
of the
Business Corporations Act
, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, which
reads as follows:

If a
corporation is the plaintiff in a legal proceeding brought before the court,
and if it appears that the corporation will be unable to pay the costs of the
defendant if the defendant is successful in the defence, the court may require
security to be given by the corporation for those costs, and may stay all legal
proceedings until the security is given.

[
10
]

The court also has inherent jurisdiction to
order a party to post security for costs.

[
11
]

The first stage of the legal test on an
application for security for costs is the requirement that the applicant make
out a
prima facie
case that the respondent would be unable to pay the
applicant’s costs if the respondent’s claim fails:
Citizens for Foreign Aid
Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4
th
)
266 B.C.S.C., 91 A.C.W.S. (3d) 362;
Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golfcourse Ltd.

(1997),
1997 CanLII 4037 (BC CA)
, 29 B.C.L.R. (3d) 252, 90 B.C.A.C. 170; and
Fat
Mel’s Restaurant Ltd. v. Canadian Northern Shield Insurance Co.
(1993)
1993 CanLII 1669 (BC CA)
, 76
B.C.L.R. (2d) 231 (C.A.), 25 B.C.A.C. 95.

[
12
]

If the applicants do meet this requirement, the
respondent may resist an order for security for costs by showing that it has
sufficient exigible assets to satisfy an award of costs:
Scopeset Technology
Inc. v. Astaro Corp.
,
2004 BCSC 830
.

[
13
]

As well, the respondent to a security for costs
application can resist an order for security for costs if it can show there is
no arguable defence to its claim:
Scopeset
at para. 15.

[
14
]

In addition, there are other factors which may
touch upon the exercise of the court’s discretion in determining whether or not
to grant an order requiring a party to post security for costs.  Potentially
relevant on the facts of this application are the following factors:

a)

Where the court is satisfied that ordering
security for costs would unfairly stifle a valid claim, the court may refuse to
order security:
Kropp

at para.
17
;

b)

Where the security for costs application is
brought against a defendant advancing a counterclaim, and the counterclaim is
sufficiently intertwined with the defendant’s defence of the main claim:
Gray
v. Powerassist Technologies Inc.
,
2001 BCSC 1208
, 10 C.P.C. (5
th
)
148 (B.C.S.C.), and
Scotford Electrical & Technical Services Ltd. v.
Blue Mountain Log Sales Ltd.
,

2005 BCSC 538
, 10 C.P.C. (6
th
)
237 (B.C.S.C., Master);  and

c)

Where the financial hardship that may give rise
to the respondent’s inability to pay costs is due to the very actions of the
applicants at issue in the respondent’s claim:
Tour-Mate Technologies Corp.
v. Syntronix Systems Limited et al.
,
1993 CanLII 2250 (BC SC)
, [1993] B.C.J. No. 599 (S.C.); and
Middlekamp
v. Fraser Valley Real Estate Board
,
[1993] B.C.J. 2965 (S.C.)
.

[
15
]

Finally, if the court concludes a security for
costs order is warranted, the court has discretion as to the quantum of
security.

ISSUES

[
16
]

The general issues on this application are as
follows:

1.

Have the applicants made out a
prima facie

case that Leduc would be unable to pay their costs if its counterclaim fails?

2.

Has Leduc shown that it has exigible assets that
could satisfy an award of costs?

3.

Has Leduc shown that the applicants do not have
arguable defences to the counterclaim?

4.

Will an order for security for costs stifle
Leduc’s ability to prosecute its counterclaim?

5.

Is the claim by ICL against Leduc sufficiently
intertwined with the Leduc counterclaim as to make it unjust to require Leduc
to post security for costs?

6.

Is the financial hardship of Leduc due to the
very actions of the applicants at issue in the counterclaim?

7.

If security for costs is to be ordered, what
should be the terms of the order including the quantum of costs?

ANALYSIS

Have the applicants made out a
prima
facie
case that Leduc would be unable to pay their costs if its
counterclaim fails?

[
17
]

The evidence on this application establishes
that Leduc has only one asset, the development property in Fort Nelson that is
the subject of this litigation.  That property is under foreclosure at the instance
of a second mortgagee.  Leduc does not appear to have any other active business
or income.

[
18
]

There is no up-to-date appraisal evidence to
establish the current market value of this residential development.  In
addition, Leduc owes just over $1 million to its investors, which is unsecured.

[
19
]

On the evidence of Leduc, one could estimate the
current market value of the Fort Nelson property to be in the range of $1.8
million but this evidence is weak and highly speculative.  If the value were
$1.8 million, there is not enough equity in the property, after paying the
secured debt, to also pay the outstanding unsecured debt of Leduc.

[
20
]

I am satisfied that ICL and L & M have made
out a
prima facie
case that their costs, if successful in defending
Leduc’s counterclaim, would be unrecoverable.

Has Leduc shown that it is has exigible
assets that could satisfy an award of costs?

[
21
]

Based on the same analysis of the evidence as
set out above, I conclude that Leduc has not shown that it has exigible assets
that could satisfy an award of costs.

Has Leduc
shown that the applicants do not have arguable defences to its counterclaim?

[
22
]

A forensic assessment of the merits of a claim
or a defence is not appropriate on an application for security for costs.

[
23
]

This is a complicated case and Leduc is prepared
to concede that ICL has an arguable defence to its counterclaim.

[
24
]

However, Leduc says that L & M does not have
an arguable defence because it has only filed a general denial at this stage of
the proceeding.

[
25
]

The statement of defence filed by L & M
simply denies the allegations in the amended counterclaim.  The only admitted
facts are that L & M is a BC incorporated company that carries on business
as professional engineers providing engineering and project management services.
All other allegations are flatly denied without any material facts being
pleaded.

[
26
]

Leduc suggests that a general denial does not
establish an arguable defence, and puts it this way in its written argument:

While this is a sufficient compliance with
the rules governing the contents of a statement of defence, it is bad practice
for the reasons pointed out by Mr. Justice Smith in his majority judgment in
Patym
Holdings Ltd. v. Michalakis

2005 BCCA 636
at paragraph
[46]
:

“His client will not be permitted to prove
material facts that differ from those alleged by the plaintiff (Rule 19(20))
nor any material facts in confession and avoidance upon which the client may
wish to rely, any facts that might take the plaintiff by surprise, or any
issues of fact not arising out of the statement of claim (Rule 19(15)).”

[
27
]

While the threshold for establishing an arguable
defence is quite low for the purposes of a security for costs application, I
agree with Leduc that L & M’s statement of defence does not meet that low
threshold.  More is required than a simple general denial.  As such, I conclude
that Leduc has established that L & M does not have an arguable defence to
its counterclaim, at this stage of the proceeding.  I am therefore satisfied
that on this ground Leduc may avoid an order for security for costs in respect
of its counterclaim against L & M.

Will an order for security for costs
stifle Leduc’s ability to prosecute its counterclaim?

[
28
]

Leduc has filed evidence that it owes over $1
million to its investors.  It has put forward evidence that its president and
sole shareholder has made shareholder loans to the company by selling his own
personal assets.  Leduc has already attempted to raise funds by a second
mortgage financing but that mortgagee has foreclosed and has conduct of sale of
its only asset, the Fort Nelson property.  The evidence is that the company’s
president and sole shareholder does not have the means to post security for
costs and has already tapped into his resources for this project by way of the
original loans from investors.

[
29
]

There is sufficient evidence in this case from
which I can conclude that Leduc is likely to be stifled in its ability to
proceed with the counterclaim if it is required to post security for costs.
This may change if the second mortgagee is able to sell the property at a price
which results in some net proceeds payable to Leduc.

Is the claim by ICL against Leduc
sufficiently intertwined with the Leduc counterclaim as to make it unjust to
require Leduc to post security for costs?

[
30
]

Both the claim by ICL and the defence and
counterclaim by Leduc against ICL turn on the relationship between those two
parties in connection with the failed development in Fort Nelson.  Both the
claim and the counterclaim will require a review of the contract or contracts
between the parties and any alleged breaches of contract and consequential
damages.

[
31
]

It must be kept in mind that this action was
commenced by ICL, the applicant on this security for costs application.  Leduc
is entitled to defend this action fully on the merits, and should not be
precluded from doing so by virtue of a security for costs order.

[
32
]

Further, it is likely that the majority of the
costs to ICL of prosecuting its claim, and in dealing with any defence by
Leduc, will be incurred in any event whether or not the counterclaim proceeds.

[
33
]

In my view, the following analysis of Joyce J.
in
Gray v. Powerassist Technologies Inc.
at para.
29
applies equally to
the case at bar:

In my opinion,
the claim and counterclaim are so intertwined that it would constitute an
injustice to permit the claim to proceed while stifling the ability of the
defendants to pursue a counterclaim is founded on the same facts upon which the
defence is dependent.  While the claim and counterclaim clearly have some distinct
features, particularly with respect to the nature of quantum of damages, both
proceedings have their genesis in the same agreement and its termination.  Both
proceedings depend on a determination of which of the two parties was at fault
in the termination of the agreement.

[
34
]

Where Leduc was brought into the action as a
defendant and advances its counterclaim in part as based on facts which also
form its defence, I am of the view that it would be unfair to require it to
post security for costs as this may well stifle its ability to respond to the
claim against it.

[
35
]

I consider this factor to weigh heavily against
an order for security for costs in this case.

Is the financial hardship of Leduc due
to the very actions of the applicants at issue in the counterclaim?

[
36
]

Leduc has filed evidence to suggest that its
current dire financial straits are due to the wrongful actions of the
defendants by counterclaim which are the very subject of the counterclaim.
This is contested on the evidence by ICL.  Leduc and ICL each has voiced
objections to the admissibility of the other’s affidavit evidence.

[
37
]

ICL has conceded that it is not appropriate on
this application for the Court to determine the merits of either side’s
position on this point, namely whether or not Leduc’s difficult financial
position is due to the wrongful actions of the defendants by counterclaim.  I
conclude that the issue is hotly contested, and on the evidence I am not able
to say whether one side or the other has a very strong case on this point.

[
38
]

This is a difficult case because it appears that
Leduc is a one- project company, and the failure of that project is the very
subject of this litigation.  If the failure of the project is due to Leduc’s
mismanagement and not the fault of the defendants by counterclaim, the
defendants by counterclaim will suffer hardship in the sense that they will
unlikely be able to recover their costs if they are successful in this
lawsuit.  On the other hand, if the failure of the project was due to the
alleged wrongful acts of the defendants by counterclaim, then Leduc will suffer
hardship if it is prevented from proceeding with its counterclaim because of an
order for security for costs which it cannot fulfil.

[
39
]

I am of the view that what tips the balance on
this difficult scale of hardship, is the fact that Leduc has been brought into
this litigation as a defendant by ICL.  As such, given the fact that the
counterclaim is intertwined with ICL’s claim against Leduc, I am of the view
that it would be unjust to not allow Leduc to fully defend and in doing so also
advance its related counterclaim.  In exercising my discretion, I am also
mindful of the fact that ICL is already in an enviable position as a litigant,
in that it has security for its claim and for some costs already posted,
totalling in excess of $300,000.

[
40
]

In coming to this conclusion, I have weighed the
factor that Leduc may be stifled in its defence and counterclaim if required to
post security for costs.  This situation could change if Leduc comes into
assets on the sale of the Fort Nelson property.  If that were to occur, an
order for security for costs might then be appropriate depending on the
circumstances.

CONCLUSION

[
41
]

The applications by ICL and L & M for an
order requiring Leduc to post security for costs in respect of the Leduc
counterclaim are dismissed on the terms that:

1.

Leduc must give notice to the defendants by counterclaim
on the distribution of the net proceeds of the sale of the Fort Nelson
property, and

2.

Leduc must preserve any funds it receives on that
distribution to allow for the notice and 14 days following the notice; and

3.

The defendants by counterclaim will have liberty
to re-apply if the circumstances change.

[
42
]

Costs will be in the cause.

Griffin
J.
